title: Ghost-squash KV anchors and sticky-slot prefetch for inter-request cache reuse
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: Requests frequently contain overlapping leading context (system prompts, user personas, short templates) that do not align perfectly with existing KV entries and cause redundant GPU work or premature eviction. Existing dedupe approaches (exact fingerprinting) miss near-duplicates and small token variations, leading to wasted compute and increased memory churn.

Goal: Implement a two-part approach to increase inter-request KV reuse without increasing tail latency: 1) Ghost-squash KV anchors — lightweight, approximate anchors that represent canonicalized leading-context signatures and allow fast hit/miss routing into larger canonical entries; 2) Sticky-slot prefetch — heuristics to keep hot anchors resident in a small set of reserved GPU slots and prefetch associated KV slices when routing predicts near-future reuse.

Success criteria:
- End-to-end token compute saved across representative workloads: >= 15% on average, >= 10% for tail-99 workloads.
- End-to-end tail-99 latency regression <= 5% compared to baseline.
- Additional GPU memory overhead for ghost anchors + prefetch metadata <= 6% at 95th percentile.
- No correctness regressions for generation outputs (automated eval on 5k prompt set, BLEU/ROUGE/semantic drift thresholds).

Design highlights:
- Anchor creation: normalize and canonicalize leading context (strip low-information tokens, normalize timestamps, fold stable fields) then compute locality-sensitive hash (LSH) plus short fingerprint. Anchors are small, CPU-resident descriptors that map to candidate canonical KV slices.
- Ghost-squash entry: a compact GPU-resident placeholder containing a pointer to candidate canonical slice(s), a small similarity score, and an occupancy credit. Ghost entries are designed to be cheap to allocate and evict; they are used to short-circuit attention/kvcache lookup when similarity is high.
- Sticky-slot prefetch: maintain a tiny reserved set of slots per worker (configurable 4-16) that prefer anchors with high reuse credit. When a request routes to a worker, the scheduler consults anchor LSH buckets and issues background prefetch of the canonical KV slices into the sticky slots if reuse probability > threshold. Prefetch uses low-priority GPU copy paths to avoid interfering with foreground inference.
- Credit ledger and eviction: implement age-weighted crediting (recent hits gain more credit) and ghost-squash special-case penalty for anchors that mispredict (to prevent noisy anchors staying sticky). Eviction integrates with existing slab allocator and respects tenant isolation budgets.
- Continuous batching interaction: sticky slots are honored by the batching layer — when an incoming request in a batch references a sticky anchor, the batch fuse path marks the KV reads as cached and uses fast GPU-local index paths to avoid full KV reconstruction. Batching telemetry is augmented to record sticky-hit rates and prefetch contention events.

Risk and trade-offs:
- Prefetch misprediction can waste memory and bandwidth; mitigated by conservative thresholds, backoff, and a metrics-driven rollback.
- Ghost anchors add another metadata layer; complexity kept small by strict size budget and reuse heuristics.
- Multi-tenant fairness: sticky slots are partitioned by tenant weight; we add guardrails to lower-priority tenants.

Planned experiments:
- Microbench: synthetic workload with controlled anchor overlap to measure hit/miss mechanics and memory overhead (lab test).
- Prod shadow: route 2% traffic to workers with feature disabled/enabled in parallel and collect cost/latency/quality metrics for 2 weeks.
- Canary: gradual rollout to 10% of capacity with runtime flag, monitor SLOs and error budget.

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Ghost-Squash+Anchors+Design
- Benchmark dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/kv/ghost-squash-experiments
